chunks: What can trigger an ISR. The question: What can trigger ISRs?
Almost any event inside or outside a microcontroller can trigger an interrupt.

Sources include a pin changing state, a timer reaching its count, a serial port receiving a byte, an analog-to-digital converter finishing a measurement, a clock failing, and the processor itself reporting a fault.
Often several sources share one handler, which must read a status register (a set of flag bits) to find out which one fired.
Imagine a building alarm panel with one shared bell. When the bell rings, the guard looks at the panel to see which light is on, deals with it, and resets that light.
Some alarms latch: the light stays on after the door closes until the guard resets it. Others follow the sensor: the light is on only while the door is open.
If the guard forgets to fix a following alarm, the bell keeps ringing.
Three families: pins, peripherals, and the core and system blocks.
All end up as a request line into the same controller ("How interrupts work and are implemented"), which is why the handling is uniform even though the origins differ.
Status flag: a bit that records which event happened. Edge-triggered: the request comes from a change, such as low to high, and is latched until cleared.
Level-triggered: the request stays active as long as the condition holds. The handler must remove the cause. Shared vector: several sources using one handler.
A serial port can interrupt for a received byte, an empty transmit buffer, or an overrun error (a new byte arrived before the last was read).
One handler reads the status register once. It handles each flag that is set and enabled: read the byte, send the next one, count the error. It clears only the flags it handled.
Now three sensors share one interrupt wire. The wire goes low if any sensor pulls it low.
With an edge trigger, a second sensor that pulls it low while the wire is already low creates no new edge, so its event is lost.
A level trigger keeps requesting until every sensor is serviced. That is the whole idea.

"Almost any event: an external pin edge or level, timer overflow, compare or input capture, UART or SPI or I2C events like byte received and transfer complete, ADC conversion complete or out-of-range, comparator output, DMA complete, RTC alarm, watchdog early warning, brown-out, plus software-triggered interrupts like PendSV and CPU faults.
Sources can be edge or level triggered, and many flags share one vector, so the ISR reads the status register to see which one fired and clears it."
